1107.title: Samantabhadra
1107.hook: the bodhisattva of practice and great vows
1107.howItsDone: In East Asian Buddhism the vows of Samantabhadra are recited in temples and at home, and Samantabhadra is shown on a white elephant, often beside Manjushri on his lion.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Manjushri, and a silence that won the day. Your line: the sword of wisdom. And now, a new week.

When space itself comes to an end, my vow will come to an end. But space never ends, so neither will the vow. That, in paraphrase, is the refrain at the close of a vast Mahayana sutra, and the one speaking it is a bodhisattva named Samantabhadra. A promise with no expiry date. Not a resolution that fades by February. A vow as wide as the sky, repeated until it sinks in.
screen: `WHEN SPACE ENDS, THE VOW ENDS.` → `SPACE NEVER ENDS.` → `NO EXPIRY DATE.`

segments.voice: First, the pair. In some Chinese temples the Buddha sits with a bodhisattva on either side: Manjushri on a lion, and Samantabhadra on a white elephant. Wisdom and practice, side by side. The elephant suits practice: slow, steady, very hard to push off the road. Second, the vows. The Flower Ornament Sutra, the Avatamsaka, ends with Samantabhadra setting out his great vows. In paraphrase: to honor all the Buddhas; to praise them; to make offerings; to admit and turn from the harm one has done; to rejoice in the good done by others; to ask the Buddhas to teach; to ask them to stay in the world; to follow their example; to meet every being where they are; and to give away the merit of everything, for the good of all. After each comes the same refrain about space and its endlessness. Third, the small one in the big list: the fifth, rejoicing in the good done by others. Being glad when a coworker gets the praise, or a sister's life goes better than yours. In the sutra it stands right beside honoring all the Buddhas, with the same endless vow. Practice includes the small, daily kinds. Fourth, the promise to others. In the last chapter of the Lotus Sutra, Samantabhadra arrives from far away and promises that whoever keeps and studies that sutra, he will come to them on his white elephant, to guard them and to teach them again any line they've forgotten. Practice, in that promise, is never quite done alone.
screen: `A LION AND A WHITE ELEPHANT.` · `VOWS THAT LAST AS LONG AS SPACE.` · `REJOICE IN THE GOOD OF OTHERS.` · `HE COMES TO THOSE WHO PRACTICE.` · then, large: `GREAT VOWS.`

segments.voice: Choose one small practice you could actually keep: a minute of quiet before picking up the phone, a kind word to someone you usually rush past, being glad out loud when someone else does well. Then, silently and in your own words, make it a vow, not until space ends, just today, and then today again. Rest with it, the way the elephant stands: steady, unhurried.
Samantabhadra. The bodhisattva of practice and great vows, riding a white elephant, whose vows last as long as space. Today's word.
Your line: great vows. As wide as space, and kept one day at a time. See you tomorrow.

1108.title: Maitreya
1108.hook: the coming Buddha, honored in Theravada and Mahayana alike
1108.howItsDone: Buddhists in Theravada and Mahayana lands honor Maitreya as the Buddha to come; some dedicate merit in the hope of meeting him, and in China images of the laughing Budai stand at temple entrances.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Samantabhadra on his white elephant, and vows as wide as space. Your line: great vows.

A Pali sutta tells a long, dark story about the world going downhill. People grow more violent. Theft spreads, then killing, then lying, and lives grow shorter and shorter. Then, at the bottom, something turns. People look at one another and decide to stop killing. Lives lengthen again. Slowly, the world grows good. And at that time, the Buddha says, another Buddha will arise, named Metteyya, teaching the same teaching he taught. Year two told this story. Today, the one it points to.
screen: `THE WORLD GOES DOWNHILL.` → `PEOPLE STOP KILLING.` → `ANOTHER BUDDHA WILL ARISE.`

segments.voice: First, a shared figure. Maitreya is the Sanskrit name; in Pali, Metteyya. He's named in the Pali texts that Theravada Buddhists keep, and honored across the Mahayana too. Schools differ on a great deal; here is one hope they hold in common. Second, where he waits. Tradition says Maitreya now lives as a bodhisattva in the Tushita heaven, where, the stories say, the bodhisattva who became Gotama Buddha waited before his last birth. He isn't a Buddha yet. He's preparing. Third, the faces. Some statues show Maitreya seated with both feet on the ground, as if about to stand up and come. And in China a wandering monk from the stories, round-bellied and laughing, a cloth sack over his shoulder, came to be seen as one of his forms. His name is Budai. If you've seen a laughing figure at a restaurant door or a temple gate, you may have met him. Fourth, what a coming Buddha says about now. Look at the order in the Pali story. The new Buddha doesn't arrive and repair a broken world. People turn first. They give up killing, decency returns one choice at a time, and only then does Metteyya arise. The future is built out of ordinary kindness, long before anyone shining appears. Some Buddhists pray to meet Maitreya in a future life; others treat the hope as a reason to practice now. Either way, it doesn't ask anyone to sit and wait.
screen: `SHARED BY THERAVADA AND MAHAYANA.` · `WAITING IN TUSHITA.` · `FEET ON THE GROUND, READY.` · `PEOPLE TURN FIRST.` · then, large: `THE ONE TO COME.`

segments.voice: Picture a morning some years from now in a place you know, your street, your kitchen, a school down the road, just a little kinder than today: someone holding a door, a neighbor checking in, a tired person waved ahead in line. Let it get specific, with colors and voices, and notice one thing in it you could begin yourself. Then let the picture fade back into the breath.
Maitreya. In Pali, Metteyya: the Buddha still to come, honored in Theravada and Mahayana alike. Today's word.
Your line: the one to come. In the old story, people turn first. Until tomorrow.

1109.title: Ksitigarbha
1109.hook: the bodhisattva who vows to help those in the lowest realms
1109.howItsDone: In East Asia, Buddhists turn to Ksitigarbha when someone has died, and the sutra of his vows is recited for the dead; in Japan, Jizo statues by roads and in temple yards are dressed and tended by local people.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Maitreya, the Buddha still to come, and a world that turns kind before he arrives. Your line: the one to come.

A young woman's mother has died, and the daughter is afraid for her. Her mother, the story says, scorned the teaching and did harm in her life. So the daughter sells the family house, brings offerings to a temple, and weeps before an image of a Buddha. A voice tells her to go home, sit, and call on that Buddha's name. In a vision she's taken to the edge of a dark sea where beings suffer, and learns her mother has already been freed. Relief. And then she thinks of all those still in that sea.
screen: `A DAUGHTER AFRAID FOR HER MOTHER.` → `A VISION OF A DARK SEA.` → `HER MOTHER IS FREED.`

segments.voice: First, the vow. Back from the vision, before that Buddha's image, the daughter vows that through lifetimes to come she will help every being who suffers in the lowest realms. The Sutra of the Past Vows of Ksitigarbha says that, after many lives, she became the bodhisattva Ksitigarbha. A saying long linked to him puts the vow in one sharp line: not until the hells are empty will I become a Buddha. Second, the look. Where other bodhisattvas often wear crowns and jewels, in East Asia Ksitigarbha usually appears as a plain monk, head shaved, holding a staff hung with rings and a jewel that lights up the dark. Dressed for walking into hard places, not for a throne. Third, the name, usually given in English as earth store, or earth womb: the ground that holds treasure and holds seeds. The ground everyone stands on, the place no one looks at. Fourth, the roadside. In China he is Dizang; in Japan, Jizo, whose small stone figures stand by roads, on mountain paths and in temple yards, sometimes dressed in red bibs and knitted caps. Jizo is seen as a protector of travelers and of children, and families grieving a child, before birth or after, sometimes come to him with their grief. He goes to the low places, and stays. If grief is heavy for you today, you don't have to carry it alone: in the US you can call or text 988, or reach local emergency help.
screen: `THE DAUGHTER'S VOW.` · `A PLAIN MONK WITH A STAFF AND A JEWEL.` · `THE EARTH STORE.` · `JIZO AT THE ROADSIDE.` · then, large: `NOT UNTIL THE HELLS ARE EMPTY.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone in a low place right now, a friend gone quiet, a relative in a hard season, a stranger who looks worn through. Don't rush to fix anything; just stand beside them in your mind for a few breaths, the way Jizo stands at the roadside, not above them, not ahead of them, beside. Then let one plain thing that might help come to mind: a message, a meal, an hour.
Ksitigarbha. The earth store: the bodhisattva who vows to help beings in the lowest realms, called Dizang in China and Jizo in Japan. Today's word.
Your line: the earth store. The lowest ground still holds the treasure. Tomorrow, skillful means.

1110.title: The doctor who seemed to die
1110.hook: teaching shaped to the listener, like a doctor fitting the medicine to the patient
1110.carry: skillful means: the teaching fitted to the listener
1110.howItsDone: Mahayana teachers speak of skillful means when they explain why the Buddha taught different things to different people, and the parables of the burning house and the physician are told in East Asian temples and study groups.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ksitigarbha, the plain monk who goes to the low places. Your line: the earth store.

A doctor comes home from a journey and finds that his sons, while he was away, got into his medicines and swallowed poison. Some are clear-headed enough to take the cure he mixes. Others are so far gone that they refuse it; to them it smells wrong. So the doctor does something strange. He leaves again, and sends a messenger home to say their father has died. The shock clears their heads. Grieving, they take the medicine he left behind, and recover. Then he comes home. That story is from the Lotus Sutra.
screen: `THE SONS SWALLOW POISON.` → `SOME REFUSE THE CURE.` → `THE DOCTOR SENDS STRANGE NEWS.`

segments.voice: First, the idea. Upaya means a means, a method. Skillful means is teaching shaped to whoever is listening. A good doctor doesn't hand every patient the same pill. In the Lotus Sutra the Buddha is that kind of doctor: different teachings fitted to different people, at different moments, with one aim. Second, the question. This block opened with another of the sutra's parables: the father who lures his children out of a burning house with the promise of carts, then gives each one a great cart. Right after, the Buddha asks his disciple Shariputra: did that father lie? No, Shariputra says. He saved his children's lives. Even if he had given them nothing at all, it would not have been a falsehood. Third, the doctor's meaning. The sutra asks the same of the doctor who sent word of his own death, and gives the same answer. Then the Buddha says he is like that doctor. If people could always see him, they'd grow careless and stop reaching for the medicine. So he appears to pass away, and the missing makes them reach. Fourth, the limit, and an older echo. Some readers point to a limit inside the stories: the trick serves the children, never the father. And the Pali texts make the point their own way. The Buddha compares his teaching to a raft: you build it to cross a river, and once you're across, you don't carry it on your head. A teaching is a tool, made for a need.
screen: `MEDICINE FITTED TO THE PATIENT.` · `WAS IT A LIE?` · `THE DOCTOR WHO SEEMS TO DIE.` · `THE RAFT IS FOR CROSSING.` · then, large: `SKILLFUL MEANS.`

segments.voice: Think of something you know well, a recipe, a game, a hard lesson life taught you, and picture explaining it to a small child, to a tired friend at the end of a long day, and to someone who doesn't quite trust you. Notice how the words change: shorter here, gentler there, a story for the child. The thing itself stays the same; only the doorway changes.
Upaya. Skillful means: teaching shaped to the one who is listening, the way a doctor fits the medicine to the patient. Today's word.
Your line: skillful means: the teaching fitted to the listener, the way a doctor fits the medicine to the one who takes it. Until tomorrow.

1111.title: The perfection of wisdom
1111.hook: the long wisdom sutras, from eight thousand lines to one letter "a"
1111.howItsDone: Mahayana communities in East Asia and Tibet chant the Heart Sutra, and some monasteries read or recite the longer perfection of wisdom sutras on special days.

segments.voice: Yesterday, upaya: a doctor's strange news and a house on fire. Your line: skillful means.

One Mahayana sutra is named for its length: the Perfection of Wisdom in a Hundred Thousand Lines. Another is the Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines. And at the far end of the same family sits the Perfection of Wisdom in One Letter, in which the Buddha gives the whole teaching as a single sound: the letter a. Somewhere in between is a page short enough to read before the kettle boils. Same subject, wildly different sizes.
screen: `A HUNDRED THOUSAND LINES.` → `EIGHT THOUSAND LINES.` → `ONE LETTER.`

segments.voice: First, a family. The perfection of wisdom isn't one book. It's a family of Mahayana sutras with one subject: the wisdom that sees all things as empty of a fixed, separate self, and the bodhisattva who walks the path with that wisdom and with compassion. Which came first, the long ones or the short ones, is a question for historians. Second, why so many sizes. One way to hear it borrows yesterday's word. Some people have the time and the hunger for a hundred thousand lines. Some need a page. Some need one breath. The teaching shrinks or grows to fit whoever receives it, the way a doctor fits the dose. Third, the page. The Heart Sutra is the short one this path read slowly in its first year. One of its lines, in plain words: form is emptiness, and emptiness is form. The things you see and touch are real enough to bump into, and also not solid, separate things standing alone. And that open, connected way things are isn't somewhere else. It's right here, as the cup and the hand and the floor. Fourth, the letter. In the One Letter text, the Buddha says the perfection of wisdom is held in the letter a. Some teachers point out that in Sanskrit, a short a at the front of a word can turn it into its opposite: himsa is harm, ahimsa is non-harm. So one small sound can say not to every fixed idea we carry. From a hundred thousand lines to one letter, only the size of the doorway changes.
screen: `A FAMILY OF SUTRAS.` · `ONE TEACHING, MANY SIZES.` · `FORM IS EMPTINESS.` · `THE WHOLE TEACHING IN A.` · then, large: `FROM LONG TO SHORT.`

segments.voice: Take one line from the Heart Sutra, form is emptiness, emptiness is form, and say it once, slowly, in your head; no copy needed. Then look at one thing in front of you, your hand, a cup, the floor, and set the line beside it without trying to work it out. Then let even the line go, and rest with the breath, short as a single letter.
The perfection of wisdom. A family of Mahayana sutras on the wisdom that sees things as they are, from a hundred thousand lines to a single letter. Today's word.
Your line: from long to short. The whole teaching can fit in one letter. See you tomorrow.

1112.title: Mother of the Buddhas
1112.hook: the perfection of wisdom honored as the mother of all Buddhas
1112.howItsDone: In Mahayana Buddhism the perfection of wisdom is honored as the mother of the Buddhas; in some communities people bow before images of the goddess Prajnaparamita and chant her name, and the wisdom sutras are recited.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the perfection of wisdom: long sutras and short ones, all the way down to a single letter. Your line: from long to short.

A stone figure of a woman, seated, legs folded, back straight, eyes lowered. Her face is calm, the kind of calm that looks like listening. In some images like this one she holds a book, or a lotus with a book resting on it. You might guess she's a queen, or a saint, or somebody's grandmother carved from memory. She isn't a person at all. She's a teaching. The sutras from yesterday gave the perfection of wisdom a family name. They called her a mother.
screen: `A SEATED WOMAN IN STONE.` → `SHE HOLDS A BOOK.` → `SHE IS A TEACHING.`

segments.voice: First, the name. In Sanskrit, the perfection of wisdom is prajnaparamita. The Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines speaks of this wisdom as the mother of the Tathagatas, the mother of every Buddha. A Buddha isn't born a Buddha. A Buddha is someone who has come to see things as they are. The seeing comes first, so the seeing is called the mother. Second, a picture the sutra gives. A woman with many children falls ill. Her children, all of them, drop what they're doing to look after her, keep her warm, keep her safe, because she gave them life and showed them the world. The Buddhas, the sutra says, care for the perfection of wisdom the same way: not because it needs them, but because it made them. Notice the direction. The great ones serve the teaching, not the other way round. Third, the woman in stone. Later, artists gave the teaching a form: the goddess Prajnaparamita, seated in meditation. Some Buddhists bow to her image and chant her name. Others take the mother as a figure of speech, a way of saying where awakening comes from. Both are found inside Mahayana, and the sutra's words fit either. Fourth, why a mother, and not a teacher or a ruler. A mother doesn't make a child by giving orders. She carries, she waits, she lets something grow in its own time. Wisdom in these sutras works like that: not a rule you obey, but what quietly gives birth to a different way of seeing. And the one who sees owes it something.

1113.title: Four great vows
1113.hook: beings are numberless, I vow to free them; delusions are endless, I vow to end them (as chanted in Zen)
1113.howItsDone: In Zen and other Mahayana communities the four great vows are chanted together, often at the end of a meditation period, at ceremonies and at the start of retreats, each community in its own version.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the mother of the Buddhas: the perfection of wisdom, tended the way grown children tend a mother who gave them the world. Your line: the mother of Buddhas.

The last bell of the evening sit rings in a Zen hall. Nobody stands up yet. Instead, the whole room starts to chant together, in a low and even voice. The first line goes something like this: beings are numberless; I vow to free them. The second: delusions are endless; I vow to end them. Then two more lines, and the room goes quiet. Said slowly, it sounds calm. Heard closely, it sounds impossible. Numberless, and I vow.
screen: `THE LAST BELL.` → `THE ROOM CHANTS TOGETHER.` → `IMPOSSIBLE, AND VOWED.`

segments.voice: First, the four lines. English versions differ, and each community keeps its own, but the shape holds. Beings without number: I vow to free them. Delusions without end: I vow to end them. Gates of the teaching beyond measure: I vow to enter them. The Buddha's way, with nothing above it: I vow to become it. Each line names something too large, then makes a promise anyway. Second, why say something impossible. A vow you can finish is a task. A vow you can't finish is a direction, the way a compass points north without ever arriving there. The bodhisattva, earlier in this block, was one who seeks awakening for the sake of all beings. These four lines are that wish, said out loud, often, with other people. Third, why together, and again. In Zen and in other Mahayana communities, the vows are chanted at the end of a sit, at ceremonies, at the start of retreats. Said once, a vow is a decision. Said every evening, it becomes a habit of the heart, worn smooth like a stair. Fourth, where this week has been: Samantabhadra and his great vows, Maitreya, the one to come, Ksitigarbha in the lowest places, then skillful means, the perfection of wisdom and its mother. Now the vows themselves, in four lines short enough to carry. Numberless, I vow. The first word admits the size of the job. The next two start it anyway.
screen: `FOUR LINES, ONE SHAPE.` · `A VOW YOU CAN'T FINISH IS A DIRECTION.` · `SAID TOGETHER, SAID AGAIN.` · `THIS WEEK, IN FOUR LINES.` · then, large: `NUMBERLESS, I VOW.`

segments.voice: Take the four vows on four breaths, in your community's version if you chant them, or just letting the shapes pass through if you don't. On each out-breath: numberless; endless; beyond measure; nothing above it. Then sit with whatever's left, the size of it, and the small steady breath that keeps going anyway.
Four great vows. Beings, delusions, gates of the teaching, the Buddha's way: each too large, each vowed anyway. Chanted in Zen halls after the sit. Today's word.
